runs.text: com os pès, o que tambem ſe diz,

lines.note: This continues the preceding definition: the action is done with the feet and is also called Fanuru. The phrase is a continuation, not an independent Portuguese entry.
Fanecaqe introduces shifting a burden or responsibility onto someone else. Its q belongs to the Japanese spelling; the Portuguese definition continues through the next two lines.

runs.text: o que hum tinha à ſua conta, ou ſobre ſi, ou por

lines.note: The burden was previously one's own responsibility. À sua conta and sobre si explain responsibility rather than merely the physical position of an object.
Por lhe a culpa makes the figurative sense explicit: blaming someone. Are coſo starts the Japanese example, while jucuxiuo- continues onto the next row.
The example accuses that person of eating the ripe fruit. Fanecaqeôzure expresses the projected accusation; Fab. is a citation label, not part of the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: imporei àquelle que elle he o que comeo os figos

lines.note: Imporei is the future 'I shall impute', matching the Japanese example better than importei. The enlarged scan supports imporei. The Portuguese calls the fruit figs; do not rewrite Japanese jucuxi to match that gloss.
Maduros completes figos maduros, 'ripe figs'. This short row belongs entirely to the translation of the preceding example and must not be read as a new entry.
Fanecayexi is a return or reversal, here with a retaliatory sense. The printed stem and inflectional forms belong together; the Portuguese comparison continues below.

runs.text: mo vingandoſe. ¶ Item, Virar de baixo

lines.note: Vingandoſe completes 'as if taking revenge'. Item then adds a physical sense of turning something over, rather than another interpretation of the retaliation example.
The additional sense is turning from underneath upwards or overturning. Reuoluer is an old spelling corresponding to revolver; no modern spelling substitution is needed.
Fanecoxi means passing or leaping over something. Read the Japanese compound in relation to 越す, while preserving the printed xi spelling and the following inflectional forms.
Dalgũa couſa completes the object of passing or jumping over. This row supplies no separate Japanese phrase; its tilde and spacing remain scan evidence, not grammatical normalization targets.
Fanecoye is the corresponding 'leap over' form, with Idem referring back to Fanecoxi. The change from xi to ye is meaningful morphology, not an interchangeable OCR spelling.

Fanecurui describes jumping about or frolicking. Its Portuguese gloss starts with brincar and continues with kicking below; the inflectional annotation should not be expanded into an unattested paradigm.
Couçes supplies the kicking component of the previous definition. Retain the printed historical ç and punctuation rather than correcting the word to a modern dictionary form.
Fanefazzuxi is prying or dislodging something. The Japanese has the hazusu-type element, and the Portuguese explicitly describes removing or dismantling rather than simply jumping.
The action uses a stick or lever. Faxiuoba begins the example about a bridge, with fane- continued by the following row's fazzuxi.
Fazzuxi completes the split verb. Taif., book 20, labels the cited example; Deſmãchan- begins the Portuguese explanation and is not part of that title.

runs.text: do a ponte com meter hum pao como lauanca

lines.note: The bridge is dismantled by inserting a stick as a lever. Ponte supports understanding Faxi as 橋 here, rather than another Japanese word with the same romanization.
Por baixo specifies insertion from below. The row completes the bridge example and should remain attached conceptually to it even though Level 1 preserves the physical line break.
Fane mocco names a basket or similar carrier. The definition is of equipment used for carrying and tipping material, not the unrelated mocco-shaped decorative motif.

runs.text: q̃ acarretão terra, pedras, &c. & ſe ſacode,

lines.note: Earth, stones and similar material are carried in the basket. The abbreviation q̃ belongs to the Portuguese prose; it does not call for Japanese kana conversion.
The carrier is shaken or tipped to empty it. Pincha and deſpejar describe the discharge of its contents, completing the practical explanation of Fane mocco.

runs.text: Balde com que tirão agua do

lines.note: Fanetçurube is a water-lifting bucket apparatus. The tsurube element is supported by balde, and the next line explains where the water is drawn from.

runs.text: poço, ou do rio, ou mar à maneira de bomba.

lines.note: The water may come from a well, river or sea. Cainte is an unfamiliar comparison term retained as printed; identifying the precise apparatus would require further Portuguese lexical evidence.
Fanevocoxi describes levering stones out. The Japanese okosu-type component agrees with arrancar, and the following example illustrates a stone too large to move directly.
The definition specifies an alauanca, a lever. Gorocujùnin begins the example's group of people; do not regularize its accent merely from a modern kana interpretation.

runs.text: temo voxi fataraqi gataqi dai banja-

lines.note: The people have difficulty pushing or moving the great rock. Dai banja- continues onto the next line, so the physical break must not suggest two separate lexical units.

The example continues the large-rock description and the collective levering action. Ycitǒ is an unusual printed spelling; its role suggests a collective expression, but it should not be silently normalized.

The enlarged scan supports the shorter citation label Tai., book 23, rather than supplying the f of the usual Taif. The translation starts 'fifty or sixty men'; its last word is worn near the right rule, so homeẽs remains a provisional reading there.

runs.text: que tinhão dificuldade em mouer hũa grande

lines.note: The men had difficulty moving a large stone. This supports the Japanese example's description of the effort, rather than introducing a second definition of the headword.

runs.text: pedra que alli auia, & finalmente com alauã-

lines.note: The stone was present there, and finally levers were used. Alauã- joins the next row's cas; the nasal mark and line division are physical features to preserve.

runs.text: cas todos a hũa ſalameando a arrãcarão.

lines.note: Together they levered the stone out. Todos a hũa supplies the collective action suggested by the Japanese example, though it does not by itself settle the unusual spelling ycitǒ.
Faneuotoxi describes throwing off or knocking down. The sentence continues with the horse's kicking action and the person sitting on it, so the Portuguese should be read as a whole.

runs.text: do couces ao que eſta em cima. ¶

lines.note: The horse throws off its rider by kicking. Cobe- starts a separate Japanese example: the enlarged scan supports this Japanese head-word element, not Portuguese Cabe-.

runs.text: Dar com a cabeça fora a

lines.note: Uo completes Cobeuo, 'the head' plus the object particle. Faneuotoſu and the Portuguese cabeça confirm the connection; the old çuo reading incorrectly mixed Portuguese and Japanese spelling.
Cortandolha explains that the person's head is cut off. This completes the Cobeuo example and resolves the sense of the preceding 'head outside/off' wording.
Faneyaburi means breaking or destroying. The verb's yaburu element is consistent with both Portuguese alternatives; the instruments or means are specified in the next row.

runs.text: algũa couſa com os pès, pao, &c.

lines.note: The destruction can be with the feet, a stick, and so on. Preserve pès as printed rather than replacing it with the modern acute-accent spelling.
Fangacu is incomplete or halfway study. Fangacuna begins its adjectival application to a person, which the following two rows explain more fully.

runs.text: Peſſoa q̃ ainda eſta no meio de ſeus

lines.note: The person is still in the middle of their studies. Mono belongs to Fangacuna mono, not to the Portuguese sentence that follows it.

runs.text: eſtudos, ou imperfeito, ſem ter acabado.

lines.note: The explanation emphasizes that the studies are unfinished or imperfect. This makes 'half learned' a better contextual gloss than an exact numerical half of a curriculum.

Fangai names a ship's compartment or cabin. Camarote makes the general sense clear, but the second Portuguese noun, currently bilj, remains visually and lexically uncertain; do not invent a confident expansion.
Fangocu is half a kingdom or territory. The fan- element here has its transparent 'half' value, unlike the unrelated animal-action compounds earlier in the column.

runs.text: Certo cheiro, ou perfume no meo

lines.note: Fangoncǒ names an aromatic substance or incense. The following explanation connects it with visions of the dead, consistent with a 'returning souls' interpretation rather than an ordinary culinary fragrance.

runs.text: do qual os gentios cuidauão na China que vião

lines.note: The dictionary reports a belief attributed to people in China. Cuidauão frames it as what they thought they saw, not as the narrator's assertion that the phenomenon occurred.
The supposed visions were of the souls of deceased people. This completes the historical explanation of Fangoncǒ; the line contains no new Japanese headword.
Fangonxô is glossed by Mexino nochino cane, a bell after a meal. Cane is Japanese 鐘 here, not the Portuguese noun cane; sino confirms its role.
The bell is rung after eating. De pois is left with the printed spacing, and the row completes the previous headword's definition.
Fangue is a medicinal substance. The brief Portuguese definition does not identify the plant precisely enough to add a confident botanical identification to Level 1.
Fanguet is half a moon, with Nacarazzuqi as its Japanese explanation. The scan supports ra rather than ta; the half-month/moon context independently supports that reading.

runs.text: ¶ Item, hũa mea Lũa q̃ poem os Iapões ſobre

lines.note: Item adds a crescent-shaped object worn or mounted by Japanese people. The phrase continues below to specify helmets and the tips of spears.

runs.text: os capacetes, & nas pontas das lanças.

lines.note: The crescent ornament is placed on helmets and spear points. This is an object shaped like the moon, not a second astronomical observation.
Fangui refers to printing or an impression. Fã- starts an example continued on the next line; the nasal abbreviation should not be expanded in the diplomatic text.
The two examples describe making a print. Suritçuquru has the tsukuru element; the enlarged scan supports q rather than g, resolving the implausible ſuritçuguru reading.
Imprimir completes the Portuguese word broken as Im- on the previous row. Although very short, it is ordinary body text, not page furniture.
Fanguin is half a cate, a unit of weight. The definition is metrological; it should not be interpreted as half of the printing process described above.
Fanguiǒ is equated with Fan, a sign or seal. The i, acts as an explanatory abbreviation; it is not a Japanese syllable to append to the headword.

Fanguiri names short or partial trousers. The enlarged scan supports Yonobacama, though the round vowels are worn; NINJAL independently lists that headword elsewhere. The bakama ending and the Portuguese garment definition support the correction from Yonchacama.

runs.text: ẽs de Iapão que traz a gente baixa.

lines.note: The trousers are worn by lower-status people according to the definition. Calço- joins ẽs across the physical break; preserve that lineation and historical nasal spelling.

runs.text: Tina larga, & baixa que ſerue pera

lines.note: A second Fanguiri is a broad, shallow tub. The next row says it serves for wine, distinguishing this homograph from the clothing entry above.
O vinho completes the tub definition. The separately marked &c. fragment is displaced material; retain its physical position rather than treating all visible text as one uninterrupted sentence.
Fangiô means half a Tatami or half a hand of paper. Tatami is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese; its typeface is scan evidence, not something to infer from language alone.
Fangiǒ is explained as half of Xechô. The Portuguese starts with half a stick of ink, and the next row adds half a sheet of paper.
The additional half-sheet definition completes the preceding entry. Pão de tinta is a shaped ink stick or cake here, not ordinary bread.
Fanifuno coya is a poor farmer's dwelling. Coya is the hut element; the precise historical interpretation of Fanifu is not established by this short gloss alone.
Fanji is glossed as Nacarajini, half dead. The example is physically split as Fan- / ji and continues with a paired expression on the next line.
Fanji fanjǒno teide aru describes being in a half-dead state. The paired terms are semantically related, and the Portuguese explanation continues below.
The person appears half dead. Vide, Fanxi is a cross-reference, so Vide is Portuguese apparatus rather than part of the Japanese expression.
Another Fanji is Fantoqi, half an hour. This is a separate time sense, not the half-dead noun from the preceding entry.
Fanji, zuru, ita introduces a verb of discussing or judging. The inflectional forms belong to the verb, distinguishing it from the preceding nominal homographs.
The gloss adds reasoning and explaining. X. is a usage label rather than an independent Japanese word; Item starts a further interpretation sense.
The further sense is interpreting dreams. Yumeuo supplies 'a dream' as object, while fanzu- continues as ru below to make the example's verb.
Ru completes fanzuru. Item then adds divination by casting lots; this is another related sense rather than a continuation of the dream's Japanese wording.
Sortes completes the divination expression. This short continuation should stay as its own physical row even though the Portuguese sentence began above.
Fanjin is Mino fanbun, half the body. The definition establishes the bodily rather than social sense of jin in this entry.
Chǔbude fanjin canauanu describes inability to use half the body through illness. The Portuguese explanation begins with não poder, split across rows.

runs.text: der menear meo corpo por doença de parleſia.

lines.note: The illness is described as parleſia, paralysis. That context supports understanding the Japanese example as impaired movement, without requiring a modern medical diagnosis.
Fanjit means half a day. The final t is part of the historical Japanese romanization and should not be treated as a missing vowel or a Portuguese abbreviation.
Fanjǒ is thriving or multiplying, with Xigueri ſacayuru as its Japanese gloss. The following example concerns descendants, clarifying the proliferation sense.
Xiſon fanjǒ ſuru refers to the increase of descendants. Crecer a geração agrees with that reading; long versus short s remains a graphic distinction rather than a semantic correction.
Multiplicar completes the preceding definition and example. It adds no independent Japanese text or new headword.
This Fanjǒ is half alive, glossed Nacara iquru. The scan supports iquru without the extra i; that historical form is compatible with the Portuguese 'estar meo viuo'.
Fanji fanjǒ repeats the half-dead/half-alive pair. The Portuguese summarizes the state as half dead, linking this entry back to the earlier Fanji example.
Fanmai is Mexino come, rice for meals or sustenance. The next row completes mantimento de arroz; the Japanese phrase should not be split into unrelated lexical guesses.
Arroz completes the food definition. It is a Portuguese continuation, not a Japanese word requiring a generated reading hint.
Fanmichi is half a league. This is a distance expression; its numerical interpretation should remain the source's rather than be converted to a modern length here.
Fanmo describes dense growth, with Xigueri as its Japanese explanation. The scan reads er- at the end, continued by uas below, giving ervas rather than the erroneous areuas.
The examples of dense growth are herbs and tree branches. Ramos daruores confirms the vegetation sense and the er- / uas reconstruction across the line break.

runs.text: Mea caxa, ou a metade de hũa

lines.note: Fanmonxen is half a caxa or half of a small coin. The next line supplies its copper material and low denomination.
The coin is a low-value copper one. This continues the money definition and should not be read as an independent description of a household object.
Fannen is Toxino fanbun, half a year. The Japanese explanatory phrase and Portuguese meo anno agree directly.

runs.text: Certas riſcas, ou veas redondas que ſe

lines.note: Fanoji names circular marks or veins. The sentence continues to specify the objects on which these patterns occur, so its object must be checked on the following row.

runs.text: fazem nas telhas, & em outras couſas.

lines.note: The scan reads telhas, roof tiles, not bilhas. This gives a plausible setting for the circular patterns while preserving the broader 'and other things' qualification.
